question: What happens when you type a URL into your browser and press Enter?
answer: The browser resolves the domain via DNS, establishes a TCP connection, negotiates TLS, sends an HTTP request, receives the response, and renders the page.
whyAsked: A classic interview question to test end-to-end understanding of the web stack. Interviewers use this to gauge depth — a junior might mention DNS and HTTP, but a strong candidate explains TCP handshakes, TLS negotiation, connection reuse, and browser rendering.
mistakes: Forgetting the DNS resolution step — it's the first thing that happens and involves multiple cache layers.
Skipping the TCP and TLS handshakes — these add latency and are critical for understanding HTTPS.
Not mentioning browser caching — the browser may not even make a network request if it has a cached response.
Forgetting that the browser makes multiple subsequent requests for CSS, JS, images, fonts, etc.
interviewPitch: When you type a URL and press Enter, the browser goes through several steps. First, it checks its **DNS cache** to resolve the domain name to an IP address. If not cached, it queries the OS cache, then the router, then ISP DNS, and finally the authoritative DNS server. Once it has the IP, the browser establishes a **TCP connection** via a 3-way handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK). If it's HTTPS (which it almost always is), a **TLS handshake** follows to negotiate encryption keys. Then the browser sends an **HTTP GET request** with headers (cookies, user-agent, accept). The server processes the request, executes backend logic, queries databases if needed, and returns an **HTTP response** (status code + headers + body). The browser receives the HTML, parses it into a **DOM tree**, fetches additional resources (CSS, JS, images, fonts) — often in parallel — builds the **CSSOM**, combines DOM + CSSOM into a **render tree**, and finally **paints** pixels on screen.
explanation:
**Step-by-Step Breakdown:**

**1. URL Parsing:**
The browser parses the URL into: protocol (`https`), domain (`www.example.com`), port (`:443` default for HTTPS), path (`/page`), query string (`?q=search`), fragment (`#section`).

**2. DNS Resolution (Domain → IP):**
Cache hierarchy checked in order:
• Browser DNS cache
• OS DNS cache (`/etc/hosts`)
• Router cache
• ISP DNS resolver (recursive)
• Root DNS → TLD DNS (.com) → Authoritative DNS → Returns IP (e.g., `93.184.216.34`)
Result is cached with a TTL (Time To Live).

**3. TCP Connection (3-Way Handshake):**
• Client → Server: **SYN** (synchronize)
• Server → Client: **SYN-ACK** (acknowledge)
• Client → Server: **ACK** (connection established)
This takes 1 RTT (Round Trip Time). Modern browsers reuse connections via **HTTP keep-alive**.

**4. TLS Handshake (HTTPS):**
• Client sends supported cipher suites
• Server responds with chosen cipher + SSL certificate
• Client verifies certificate against trusted CAs
• Both derive session keys using key exchange (e.g., ECDHE)
• Adds 1-2 RTTs. TLS 1.3 reduces this to 1 RTT (or 0-RTT with resumption).

**5. HTTP Request:**
```
GET /page HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
User-Agent: Chrome/125
Accept: text/html
Cookie: session=abc123
```

**6. Server Processing:**
Load balancer → Web server → Application code → Database queries → Response assembly.

**7. HTTP Response:**
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Cache-Control: max-age=3600
Content-Length: 5432

<!DOCTYPE html>...
```

**8. Browser Rendering:**
• Parse HTML → **DOM Tree**
• Parse CSS → **CSSOM Tree**
• Fetch external resources (CSS, JS, images) — browser may make 50+ requests
• Execute JavaScript (can modify DOM)
• Combine DOM + CSSOM → **Render Tree**
• **Layout** (calculate positions and sizes)
• **Paint** (draw pixels to screen)
• **Composite** (layer management for smooth scrolling/animations)
example:
Step-by-step with approximate latencies:

1. URL Parsing              ~0ms
2. DNS Lookup               ~20-120ms (cached: ~0ms)
   Browser cache → OS cache → Router → ISP → Root DNS → TLD → Auth DNS
   Result: www.example.com → 93.184.216.34

3. TCP Handshake            ~1 RTT (~30ms)
   Client ──SYN──→ Server
   Client ←SYN-ACK── Server
   Client ──ACK──→ Server

4. TLS Handshake            ~1-2 RTT (~60ms)
   Negotiate cipher suite + verify certificate
   TLS 1.3: ~1 RTT  |  TLS 1.2: ~2 RTTs

5. HTTP Request             ~30ms
   GET /page HTTP/1.1
   Host: www.example.com

6. Server Processing        ~50-500ms
   Routing → Controller → DB Query → Response

7. HTTP Response            ~30ms
   200 OK + HTML body

8. Browser Rendering        ~100-1000ms
   HTML → DOM → CSSOM → Render Tree → Layout → Paint
   + parallel fetches for CSS, JS, images, fonts

Total: ~300ms - 2s for a typical page load

question: What is the difference between REST and gRPC?
answer: REST uses HTTP/1.1 with JSON for human-readable APIs. gRPC uses HTTP/2 with Protocol Buffers (binary) for high-performance service-to-service communication with strongly-typed contracts.
whyAsked: Tests knowledge of modern API architectures. Interviewers want to see if you can choose the right communication protocol for microservices vs public APIs.
mistakes: Saying gRPC is always better — REST is simpler, browser-friendly, and better for public APIs.
Not knowing that gRPC uses binary serialization (Protobuf) — much faster than JSON parsing.
Thinking gRPC doesn't work in browsers — gRPC-Web exists as a bridge.
Not knowing gRPC supports streaming — bidirectional streaming is a key advantage over REST.
interviewPitch: **REST** is the standard for public APIs — it uses **HTTP/1.1**, **JSON** payloads, and follows resource-based URL patterns (`GET /api/users/5`). It's human-readable, widely supported, and browser-friendly. **gRPC** is designed for **service-to-service** communication in microservices — it uses **HTTP/2**, **Protocol Buffers** (binary serialization, 10x faster than JSON), and **strongly-typed contracts** defined in `.proto` files. gRPC supports 4 communication patterns: **unary**, **server streaming**, **client streaming**, and **bidirectional streaming**. I use REST for external/public APIs and gRPC for internal microservice communication where performance matters.
explanation:
**REST:**
• HTTP/1.1 (text-based)
• JSON or XML payloads
• Resource-based URLs: GET/POST/PUT/DELETE
• Human-readable, easy to debug with curl/Postman
• Browser-native (fetch API)
• Loosely typed (no contract enforcement)

**gRPC:**
• HTTP/2 (multiplexed, binary framing)
• Protocol Buffers (binary, ~10x smaller than JSON)
• Contract-first: `.proto` files define services
• Code generation: auto-generates client/server code
• 4 patterns: unary, server stream, client stream, bidirectional
• Not directly browser-compatible (needs gRPC-Web)

**When to use:**
• REST: public APIs, browser clients, 3rd-party integrations
• gRPC: microservice-to-microservice, real-time streaming, high throughput

**Performance:**
• gRPC is ~7-10x faster than REST for serialization
• HTTP/2 multiplexing reduces connection overhead
• Binary payload = smaller network transfer

question: What are WebSockets and how are they different from HTTP?
answer: WebSockets provide full-duplex, persistent communication over a single TCP connection. Unlike HTTP's request-response model, WebSockets allow the server to push data to clients in real-time.
whyAsked: Tests understanding of real-time communication. Interviewers want to see if you know when to use WebSockets vs polling vs SSE, and how SignalR implements real-time in .NET.
mistakes: Using WebSockets for everything — HTTP is simpler and better for standard request-response operations.
Not knowing that WebSocket connections start as HTTP then upgrade — the initial handshake is HTTP.
Forgetting connection management — WebSockets are stateful; you must handle disconnects and reconnections.
Not knowing about SignalR — it abstracts WebSockets and provides fallbacks for older browsers.
interviewPitch: **HTTP** is **request-response** — the client sends a request, the server responds, and the connection is closed (or kept alive for reuse). The server **cannot push** data without a client request. **WebSockets** upgrade an HTTP connection to a **persistent, full-duplex** TCP channel — both client and server can send messages **at any time** without waiting. This is essential for **real-time** applications: chat, live notifications, stock tickers, multiplayer games. In ASP.NET Core, I use **SignalR** which abstracts WebSockets and automatically falls back to Server-Sent Events or long polling if WebSockets aren't available. SignalR provides **hub-based programming** — clients call server methods and servers call client methods.
explanation:
**HTTP vs WebSocket:**

| Feature | HTTP | WebSocket |
|---------|------|-----------|
| Connection | Short-lived | Persistent |
| Direction | Client → Server | Bidirectional |
| Server Push | Not possible | Yes |
| Overhead | Headers per request | One handshake |
| Protocol | HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 | ws:// or wss:// |
| Use Case | CRUD APIs | Real-time data |

**Alternatives for real-time:**
• **Polling**: client calls API every N seconds (wasteful)
• **Long Polling**: server holds request until data available
• **SSE (Server-Sent Events)**: server → client only (one-directional)
• **WebSockets**: full-duplex (best for bidirectional)

**SignalR (ASP.NET Core):**
• Abstraction over WebSockets
• Auto-fallback: WebSocket → SSE → Long Polling
• Hub pattern: strongly-typed client/server methods
• Group management: broadcast to specific groups
• Scale-out with Redis backplane for multiple servers
